english: Do you know Turkish?
tip: Yes/no questions use a separate word mu: biliyor musunuz (do you know). The person ending -sunuz rides on musunuz, not on biliyor.

english: Nobody is listening to me.
tip: Kimse (nobody) still needs a negative verb: dinlemiyor (isn't listening). Turkish doubles the negative where English uses just one.

english: I usually drink tea at breakfast.
tip: içerim uses the aorist -er for habits and general facts: iç + er + im. Use it for what you usually do, not -iyor for right now.

english: Farewell, I will miss you very much.
tip: Future is stem + -ecek + person: özleyeceğim (I will miss). A y slips in as a buffer because özle ends in a vowel.

english: You read a newspaper at the office.
tip: okuyorsun (an -iyor form) covers both you are reading now and you read generally. Turkish does not split habit from ongoing action.

english: My aunt loves doing sports.
tip: yapmayı = yap + ma (turns the verb into a noun, doing) + yı (object marker). sever needs its object marked this way.

english: My daughter loves doing sports.
tip: Kızım = kız + ım (my daughter). Turkish has no separate word for my, you attach the owner onto the noun.

english: The house's roof needs to be repaired.
tip: Evin çatısı is an of-chain: Evin (of the house) plus çatısı (its roof). Both the owner and the thing take a suffix.

english: You are not right about this.
tip: değil negates nouns and adjectives, not verbs: haklı değilsiniz (you are not right). The person ending sits on değilsiniz.

english: Could you recommend a good restaurant?
tip: önerir misiniz pairs the aorist with the question word for a polite request, close to English would you recommend.

english: The doctor is examining the patient carefully.
tip: hastayı carries -yı because it is a specific, known object: the patient. A plain hasta would mean just any patient.

english: The weather is not nice, it's raining.
tip: Turkish says yağmur yağıyor (rain is raining), the noun and verb built from the same root. Standard way to say it is raining.

english: I don't know this city at all.
tip: hiç means at all only when the verb is negative: hiç tanımıyorum (do not know at all). It leans on the negative verb.

target: Bu ders kırk beş dakika sürüyor.
english: This lesson lasts forty-five minutes.
tip: sürüyor shows -iyor echoing the root vowel: sür has ü, so the suffix rounds to -üyor, not -iyor.

target: Hava durumunu kontrol ettim, yarın yağmur var.
english: I checked the weather, there's rain tomorrow.
tip: yağmur var = there is rain. var means there is or there are and needs no verb for to be. Its opposite is yok.

english: The museum was closed when we arrived.
tip: kapalıydı = kapalı (closed) + ydı (was). Add -ydı to an adjective to put it in the past, no separate verb needed.

english: I can't speak Turkish but I understand.
tip: konuşamıyorum means I cannot speak. The -ama tucked inside is the negative of ability, the opposite of -abil (can).

english: Well, I need to think about it a bit.
tip: düşünmem lazım = I need to think. Verb plus -mem or -mam plus lazım is the everyday way to say I have to.

english: We watched the football match at the café.
tip: izledik = izle + dik (we watched). Past tense adds -di plus a person ending, here -dik for we.

english: I want to visit the museums in Turkey.
tip: Türkiye'deki means the ones in Turkey. The -ki after a location turns it into an adjective describing the next noun.

english: I've been together with my spouse for twenty years.
tip: Eşimle = eş + im + le (with my spouse). The ending -le or -la attached to a noun means with.

english: Good evening, welcome.
tip: Turkish greetings take the plural -lar: akşamlar (evenings), not singular akşam. Same pattern shows up in iyi geceler.

english: The electrician fixed the broken lamp.
tip: tamir etti = fixed. Many actions are a noun plus etmek: tamir (repair) plus etti (did). The noun stays put, etmek carries tense.

english: I sweep the floor before mopping.
tip: yapmadan önce = before doing. Verb plus -madan önce means before X-ing: yapmadan önce (before mopping).

english: Can you speak more slowly, please?
tip: konuşabilir = can speak: konuş + abilir. The -abilir or -ebilir slotted onto the root means able to.

english: I wash the dishes right after eating.
tip: Yemekten takes -ten, not -den, because yemek ends in a voiceless k. After voiceless consonants the from ending hardens.

english: My father drinks tea while reading his newspaper.
tip: okurken = while reading. The ending -ken means while and attaches straight onto the verb form.

english: My uncle goes for a walk every day.
tip: yürüyüşe = yürüyüş + e (for a walk). The -e or -a ending marks where you are heading or aiming.

english: I tidy up my desk before starting work.
tip: başlamak takes the dative, so it is İşe başlamak (start work), not the object case. The verb decides the ending.

english: Get well soon, we are all thinking of you.
tip: seni = sen + i, the object form of you. The -i ending marks the definite object of düşünüyoruz (we are thinking of).
